Scenario: A newly added subnet's VMs hav: The most likely cause is Private Google Access simply not being enabled on the new subnet - unlike a VPC-wide setting, it's configured per-subnet, so the existing GKE subnet having it enabled doesn't automatically extend to a newly added subnet. Confirm via `gcloud compute networks subnets describe <subnet>` checking the `privateIpGoogleAccess` field, and enable it if it's false - also double-check firewall rules and routes aren't separately blocking egress to Google's API IP ranges (199.36.153.4/30 for private.googleapis.com or similar restricted ranges) if enabling Private Google Access alone doesn't resolve it.
Scenario: Two VPCs are peered and the pe: Check custom route export/import settings on the peering connection first - VPC Peering by default only exchanges subnet routes, not custom routes, so if VPC B's target is reachable only via a custom route (not a direct subnet route), that route won't propagate to VPC A unless custom route export/import is explicitly enabled on both sides. Also verify there's no CIDR overlap between the VPCs (peering silently fails to route correctly if ranges overlap) and check firewall rules on the receiving side (VPC B's firewall must explicitly allow ingress from VPC A's IP ranges - peering enables routing, but firewall rules still gate the traffic).
Scenario: After migrating from Cloud VPN: Check the route priorities/BGP configuration on both paths - if the VPN tunnel's routes still have equal or better priority than the Interconnect's BGP-advertised routes, traffic can load-balance or fail over between the two rather than exclusively preferring Interconnect. Confirm the Interconnect's BGP session is fully established and advertising the expected prefixes, explicitly lower the VPN's route priority (higher priority number in GCP's convention, since lower values are preferred) relative to the Interconnect path so it's used only as a genuine backup, and check for asymmetric routing (traffic going out one path and returning via the other) which can cause exactly this kind of intermittent, hard-to-reproduce behavior.
Scenario: Requests to a Global HTTPS Loa: Check whether the affected regions correspond to backends that are failing health checks intermittently (a backend flapping between healthy/unhealthy causes exactly this region-specific, intermittent symptom) - review health check logs and the backend's own capacity/utilization during the failure windows, since a backend near its capacity limit can start failing health checks under load spikes specific to that region's traffic pattern. Also check Cloud CDN cache-fill behavior if those regions serve more cache-miss traffic (a cache miss requires a full round-trip to the origin, which can expose backend capacity issues that a high cache-hit-rate region wouldn't surface as noticeably) - correlating the reset timing with backend health check status and cache hit ratio per region usually pinpoints which of the two is the actual cause.
Scenario: A VPC-native GKE cluster runs: This is an IP exhaustion problem in the cluster's secondary Pod CIDR range, not a resource problem - `kubectl describe pod` on the stuck Pod may not show it clearly, so check the cluster's Pod IP range utilization directly (via the GKE console or `gcloud container clusters describe`), which reveals if the allocated Pod CIDR range is genuinely exhausted. Since a cluster's Pod IP range size is fixed at cluster creation for the default configuration, fixing this typically requires either reducing max-pods-per-node to fit within the existing range more efficiently, migrating to a cluster with a larger Pod CIDR range, or (in newer GKE versions) using discontiguous multi-Pod-CIDR support to add additional Pod IP ranges to an existing cluster without a full rebuild.
Scenario: A Cloud Run service using a Se: Check the VPC Access connector's throughput capacity/scaling configuration first - connectors have a configurable minimum/maximum instance count and each instance has a bandwidth ceiling, so under load the connector itself can become the bottleneck if it hasn't scaled up enough instances or has hit its configured maximum. Increase the connector's max instances/throughput setting if it's under-provisioned for the actual traffic level, and separately confirm the private resource being reached (a VM, Cloud SQL) isn't itself the bottleneck under the increased connection volume the higher traffic generates.
Scenario: Firewall rules appear to block: Evaluate rules in their actual precedence order: Hierarchical Firewall Policies (organization/folder level) are evaluated first, then VPC-level firewall rules, within each level ordered by priority number (lower number = higher priority, evaluated first) - a lower-priority-number allow rule at any level can permit traffic that a higher-priority-number deny rule elsewhere would otherwise block, since the first matching rule in evaluation order wins. Use `gcloud compute firewall-rules list --sort-by=priority` and check hierarchical policies via the Resource Manager, looking specifically for an unexpectedly permissive allow rule with a lower priority number than the intended deny rule, or a rule scoped to the wrong target (network tag/service account) so it doesn't actually apply to the deny rule you expect it to interact with.
Scenario: VPC Flow Logs show a productio: Investigate first: identify the specific process/container making the connection (correlate the Flow Log's source Pod/VM IP and timestamp with application logs and, if needed, exec into the workload to inspect running processes), check what the external IP actually is (a known service, a CDN, or something unrecognized/suspicious via IP reputation lookup), and check whether this matches expected legitimate behavior (a scheduled batch job, a monitoring agent) that simply looks unusual out of context. Contain by adding an explicit egress-deny firewall rule for that destination if it's confirmed unauthorized, rotating any credentials the workload has access to if compromise is suspected, and escalating to the security team for a fuller forensic investigation rather than only blocking the connection and considering it resolved.
Scenario: Network Intelligence Center re: Connectivity Tests analyze the *configured* network path (routes, firewall rules) rather than performing a live packet test by default, so a discrepancy usually means either the configuration changed in the intervening five minutes (a firewall rule or route was modified), or the actual live path succeeded due to a specific existing connection/session (stateful firewall behavior allowing an already-established flow) that a fresh connectivity test's simulated new connection wouldn't have. Re-run the test immediately to rule out a stale test result, check for very recent firewall/route changes via Cloud Audit Logs, and if genuinely inconsistent, trust the live curl result as ground truth for present-moment reachability while treating the Connectivity Test finding as a signal to check for recent or in-progress config changes.
Scenario: After a region-level outage, D: The root problem is almost always DNS TTL and propagation delay - if the DNS record's TTL was set too high (or client-side/resolver caching ignored it), traffic kept resolving to the failed region long after the change was made. Redesign by moving off DNS-based failover entirely where possible in favor of a Global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with health-checked backends across regions (failover happens at the load balancer/anycast layer within seconds, with no DNS propagation delay at all), and if DNS-based failover must be kept for some reason, set aggressively short TTLs well before any incident (not reactively during one) and use a health-check-integrated DNS failover policy (like Cloud DNS routing policies with health checks) rather than manual DNS updates during an outage.
Scenario: You need to migrate an organiz: Re-plan CIDR ranges first, ensuring new subnets in the Shared VPC host project don't overlap with anything existing, and design service-project subnet allocation with enough room for future growth per team. Migrate firewall rules to the new Shared VPC structure in parallel (recreated and validated in the new environment, not moved destructively), and set up IAM properly (host project owns network admin roles centrally, service projects get 'Compute Network User' roles scoped to specific subnets so teams can deploy without needing network admin rights). Execute cutover incrementally - migrate one workload/team at a time onto the new Shared VPC (via new subnet attachment and updated resource creation, not moving existing running VMs in place), validating connectivity at each step, keeping the legacy flat VPC running in parallel until every workload has successfully migrated and been validated, only decommissioning it once nothing remains dependent on it.
